newsitem.title: GERMANY: Salomon judges Tokyo stocks a cautious buy.
newsitem.headline: Salomon judges Tokyo stocks a cautious buy.

text.p: The Tokyo stock market, which started 1997 with a thud that sent jitters round the world, is now looking fairly valued but cannot expect much of a rebound until 1998, Salomon Brothers Asia analysts said on Friday.

"We've started 1997 just terribly, and Tokyo stocks are now in the eighth year of a bear market. But there are fundamental and technical reasons to look for buys," Salomon's Tokyo-based equities strategist Craig Chudler told reporters ahead of a day-long presentation to European investors.

The Nikkei index of 225 stocks ended on Friday at 18,090.04, back from Monday's low of 17,019.56, but still below the lowest levels seen late last year. The index is down from 19,361.35 on December 30 and from a 1996 high of 22,750.70 on June 26.

Evaporating chances for economic growth, dashed hopes of a rebound in real-estate prices, languishing bank stocks and aggressive issuance of new equities have fuelled the weakness over the past half-year, Chudler said.

But analysts at Salomon, one of the most influential foreign brokerages in Tokyo, are beginning to shift to "buy" recommendations on selected Japanese stocks positioned to benefit from the weaker yen or the pressing need to restructure the economy.
The Nikkei should recover the 23,000 level next year as the outlook for economic growth turns sunnier again after the current cloudburst, said chief Tokyo economist Robert Feldman.

Salomon has revised down its forecast for fiscal 1997 growth in gross domestic product (GDP) to 0.7 percent from a 1.2 prediction it made last October, due to falling housing starts and public consumption, Feldman said.
Private consumption is growing more slowly than expected. But GDP growth should recover to 2.2 percent in fiscal 1998, Feldman said.

"We expect no more cuts in spending or increases in taxes (in 1998). These are the key things markets will focus on after the summer," he said. Salomon also expects no tightening of the Bank of Japan's current easy monetary policy until mid-1998.

Japan's renowned export-oriented sectors such as cars, steel and electronics are looking much more competitive with the dollar at its current level of 117 yen, up from 80 yen in April 1995, Chudler said.
Some technology stocks such as Canon and NEC have actually risen since last July despite the Tokyo downturn and the global dumping of technology shares.
Other shares in Salomon's model Tokyo portfolio include NTT, Toyota, Tokyo Mitsubishi Bank, Sankyo Pharmaceuticals and Hitachi.

Japan's beleaguered banks, which account for a full 20 percent of market capitalisation, remain hobbled by property-linked problems, but a few have fallen far enough, sector analyst Alicia Ogawa said.
"Non-performing loans have not stopped growing, and with the exception of three or four banks the outlook is quite bleak," Ogawa said.

Feldman said the main worry left hanging over the Tokyo stock market is the surging level of government debt. While Tokyo ran fiscal surpluses of three percent of GDP in the 1980s, it now has a deficit of about four percent of GDP.

Japan's outstanding government debt could swell to 150 percent of GDP in 30 years if current trends continue, he said. Tokyo authorities' past reaction to similar situations has been to raise taxes, but this would be a policy dead-end, as European governments have discovered.
"Tokyo must change its fiscal policy to reduce both expenditure and taxes," he said.
